submissions.findingTextShort: A 24-week randomized trial found dong quai monotherapy no better than placebo for menopausal symptoms or measured estrogenic effects.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial enrolled 71 postmenopausal women with hot flashes and treated them for 24 weeks with dong quai or placebo. The study found no statistically significant between-group differences in endometrial thickness, vaginal maturation index, vasomotor flush frequency, or Kupperman menopausal-symptom score; dong quai used alone was no more helpful than placebo for menopausal symptoms and did not produce the measured estrogen-like responses.
submissions.populationContext: Seventy-one postmenopausal women with hot flashes, mean age about 52 years, randomized to dong quai or placebo for 24 weeks.
submissions.usageContext: Dong quai monotherapy; this direct human null finding should constrain claims about menopausal symptom relief or estrogen-like clinical effects.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: This is one older randomized trial using a specific preparation and duration. It supports a null result for the studied menopausal outcomes, not proof that every Angelica preparation or every possible endpoint is ineffective. The source must complete registry and semantic-attestation governance before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A small randomized trial found no significant hot-flash benefit from dong quai in men receiving androgen-deprivation therapy.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled pilot trial enrolled 22 men receiving androgen-deprivation therapy for prostate cancer with bothersome hot flashes; 17 completed three months of treatment. There were no significant differences between dong quai and placebo in hot-flash severity, frequency, or duration, so this population-specific trial does not support a vasomotor-treatment benefit.
submissions.populationContext: Twenty-two men receiving luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone agonist therapy for prostate cancer; 17 completed the three-month pilot trial.
submissions.usageContext: Population-specific vasomotor-symptom evidence in men on androgen-deprivation therapy; not a menopause study and not generalizable to other Angelica uses.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Very small pilot trial with attrition and baseline imbalance in hot-flash frequency. The null finding should be preserved but not overgeneralized beyond the studied population, preparation, and three-month duration. The source must complete registry and semantic-attestation governance before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A human case report describes marked INR/prothrombin-time elevation after dong quai was added to stable warfarin therapy.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A published case report described a 46-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who had been stable on warfarin and developed a greater than two-fold increase in prothrombin time and INR after taking dong quai concurrently for four weeks. No other cause was identified in the report, and coagulation values returned to an acceptable range about one month after dong quai was discontinued.
submissions.populationContext: Single adult patient case report involving chronic warfarin therapy and four weeks of concurrent dong quai exposure.
submissions.safetyContext: Supports a clinically important warfarin-interaction caution and coagulation monitoring concern, but not an incidence estimate or certainty that every Angelica product produces the interaction.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Single-patient case evidence cannot establish population frequency, dose-response, mechanism, or universal causality. The dechallenge and absence of another identified cause strengthen the signal but do not convert it into controlled interaction evidence. The source must complete registry and semantic-attestation governance before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A menopausal trial of Dang Gui Buxue Tang is combination-specific and mostly null, so its subgroup signal cannot be assigned to Angelica alone.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A six-month randomized double-blind placebo-controlled study evaluated Dang Gui Buxue Tang, a 1:5 combination of Angelica sinensis and Astragalus membranaceus, in about 100 symptomatic women. Overall vasomotor outcomes were not significantly different from placebo; the formula was statistically superior only for mild hot flushes, while other severity, night-sweat, and quality-of-life results were null or favored placebo. Because the intervention was a two-herb formula, any observed signal cannot be attributed specifically to Angelica sinensis.
submissions.populationContext: Approximately 100 Hong Kong Chinese women with menopausal symptoms randomized to a six-month two-herb formula or placebo.
submissions.usageContext: Dang Gui Buxue Tang contained Angelica sinensis and Astragalus membranaceus in a 1:5 combination; it is not Angelica monotherapy evidence.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Mixed subgroup findings and a multi-ingredient intervention make single-herb attribution inappropriate. Preserve the overall null comparison and do not promote the mild-hot-flush subgroup signal into Angelica-specific efficacy. The source must complete registry and semantic-attestation governance before promotion.
